resources.string: Permission prompt
Android asks you in a pop-up the first time the app needs it. You can revoke it at any time: Settings > Apps > the app > Permissions.
“Allow all the time” setting
It is never granted with a single tap: you have to choose “Allow all the time” in the app\'s permissions. Switch it back to “Allow only while using the app” if in doubt.
Tied to photo access
No separate prompt: it comes with access to your photos and videos. Removing the app\'s photo access removes it too.
Special access
A powerful access you have to switch on yourself in a dedicated settings screen (Settings > Apps > Special app access). An app that sends you there needs a very good reason.
Granted automatically
It is granted automatically at install time, without any prompt, and cannot be revoked without uninstalling the app.

Screen and capture
Background location
Know your location even when the app is closed or you are not using it.

This is round-the-clock tracking: home, work, places of care, worship or dating, schedules… A few days of locations are enough to identify you and reconstruct your life. This data is highly sought after by data brokers.
Precise location (GPS)
Know your location to within a few metres while you use the app.
Essential for a GPS or a running app, but it reveals exactly where you are. For an app that only needs the city (weather, shop), approximate location is enough.
Approximate location
Know your location at neighbourhood or city level.
Less intrusive than GPS, it still reveals your regular movements and is often used for local targeting.
Photo locations
Read the GPS coordinates stored in your photos and videos.
Your photos tell where you were and when: home, holidays, places you visit. An app can retrace your past movements without ever asking for your location.
Read SMS
Read all your text messages, old and new.
Your private conversations, but also banking and login verification codes received by SMS: enough to take over accounts. Google restricts it to default SMS apps.
Receive SMS
Be notified of and read each text message as it arrives.
Lets an app intercept one-time codes as soon as they arrive, a classic technique of banking malware.
Send SMS
Send text messages on your behalf, without going through your messaging app.
Risk of premium-rate texts billed to your plan, or messages sent to your contacts without your knowledge.
Receive MMS
Receive and read MMS (messages with a photo or video).
Gives access to the content of private messages, photos included.
Call log
Read the list of your calls: numbers, dates, durations.
Who you call, when and for how long maps out your personal, medical or professional circle. Google restricts it to default phone apps.
Modify call log
Add, change or delete entries in your call history.
An app could erase the trace of calls it made or tamper with your history.
Outgoing calls
See the number you dial and redirect or cancel the call (legacy permission, removed since Android 10).
Reveals every number you call; its presence often betrays an old or poorly maintained app.
Make calls
Call a number directly, without you confirming in the Phone app.
Useful for a “call customer service” button, but also allows calls to premium-rate numbers.
Answer calls
Pick up or hang up an incoming call for you.
Legitimate for a watch or a connected car; elsewhere, an app has no reason to handle your calls.
Phone status and identity
Know whether you are on a call, your carrier, your network and information about the SIM card.
The reassuring name hides information useful for recognising you from one app to another. Tracking SDKs love it to build a device fingerprint.
Your phone number
Read the phone number of your SIM cards.
Your number is a stable, personal identifier that can be used to find you elsewhere (messaging apps, data leaks, cold calling).
Address book
Read all your contacts: names, numbers, e-mails, addresses, notes.
This is not only your data but your loved ones\' too, and they agreed to nothing. Address books are often uploaded to servers to “find friends” or feed profiles.
Modify contacts
Add, change or delete contacts.
An app can add its own entries (sales number, support) or alter yours.
Phone accounts
See the accounts registered on the phone (Google, e-mail, social networks).
Since Android 8, the app only sees its own accounts or those you entrust to it, but asking for it still signals interest in your online identity.
Microphone
Record sound through the microphone while you use the app.
Conversations, voices, background noise: the microphone picks up far more than your voice command. Android shows a green dot when it is in use; be wary if it appears for no reason.
Camera
Take photos and videos, or scan a code, while you use the app.
Normal for scanning a QR code or a document. Less so for an app with nothing to photograph. A green dot signals when it is in use.
Read calendar
Read all your appointments and those of shared calendars.
Your medical, work or personal appointments, with places and attendees, describe your life precisely, and that of the other guests.
Modify calendar
Create, change or delete events.
Handy for adding a booking, but an app can also delete or change your appointments.
Body sensors
Read health sensors: heart rate, blood oxygen, etc.
Health data is among the most sensitive there is (GDPR, article 9): it can reveal illness, stress or pregnancy.
Body sensors in the background
Read your health sensors even when the app is not open.
Permanent health monitoring, rarely needed outside a watch or medical tracking app.
Physical activity
Detect whether you are walking, running, cycling or driving, and count your steps.
Reveals your habits, journeys and lifestyle, even without access to your location.
Files and media (legacy access)
Read the photos, videos, music and documents in shared storage.
Opens access to your whole gallery and downloads. Since Android 13 it has been replaced by finer-grained access: VYLIA only counts it for apps built for older versions.
All files access
Read, modify and delete every file in shared storage, without restriction.
ID documents, statements, photos, backups: everything becomes readable. In principle reserved for file managers and antivirus apps.
Photos
Read the photos in your gallery.
Faces, photographed documents, screenshots, places: a gallery says a lot. Android 14 lets you share only selected photos; prefer that option.
Videos
Read the videos in your gallery.
Same concern as photos: your videos show people and places.
Audio files
Read your music, podcasts and recordings.
Not very sensitive for music, more so for voice memos or call recordings.
Bluetooth device scan
Detect Bluetooth devices around you (earbuds, watches, beacons).
Bluetooth beacons in shops and public places reveal where you are, even without location access.
Nearby Wi-Fi devices
Detect and connect to nearby Wi-Fi devices (printer, speaker, camera).
The list of nearby networks and devices can be used to infer your location.
List of your apps
See the full list of apps installed on your phone.

Your app list says a lot about you: a health, banking, dating, religious or political app reveals intimate information. The combination of installed apps is also a near-unique fingerprint for tracking you.
Usage statistics
Know which apps you use, when and for how long.
Your sleeping hours, habits and night-time or work usage can be read in these statistics.
Install other apps
Offer to install apps downloaded outside the Play Store.
A gateway for apps not checked by Google, or even malicious ones. Legitimate for a browser or an alternative store (F-Droid), suspicious elsewhere.
Accessibility service
Read everything shown on screen and act for you: tap, type text, navigate.

This is Android\'s most powerful access, designed to help people with disabilities. It can read passwords and messages, and it is the favourite tool of spyware. Only grant it to an accessibility app you trust.
Notification access
Read all your notifications, from every app, and dismiss them.
Message previews, e-mails, verification codes, bank alerts: everything goes through notifications.
Device administrator
Lock the phone, enforce a PIN, wipe all data, prevent uninstallation.
Legitimate for a work phone managed by your employer or an anti-theft app. Elsewhere it is excessive control, sometimes used to make an app impossible to remove.
Display over other apps
Show windows on top of other apps (chat bubbles, floating player).
A fake window can cover a real app to make you type a password or tap a button without realising.
Internet access
Send and receive data over the Internet.
Almost every app has it, and it is not counted in the score. But it is the door through which everything the app collects leaves the phone: an app without it cannot send anything.
Network status
Know whether you are connected, and whether through Wi-Fi or mobile data.
Harmless on its own: it lets an app wait for Wi-Fi before a big download.
Wi-Fi information
See the Wi-Fi network you are connected to and nearby networks.
The names of the networks around you can reveal where you are, even without location access.
Targeting ID
Read your phone\'s targeting ID, the same for every app.
It lets third-party companies recognise you from one app to another and build a profile. You can delete it: Settings > Privacy > Ads (or Google > Ads).
Install referrer
Ask the Play Store which link or campaign led you to install the app.
Used to measure marketing campaigns: it ties your installation to content you saw elsewhere.
Start at boot
Run as soon as the phone starts, without you opening the app.
Useful for an alarm clock or a messaging app. Combined with other accesses, it lets an app work in the background without you knowing.
Foreground service
Keep running in the background, with a permanent notification.
Normal for music, navigation or a call. The notification is there to warn you: if you don\'t understand it, check the app.
Notifications
Show notifications.
Not a privacy risk, but often a way to bring you back into the app. You can refuse it or limit it per notification category.
Keep the phone awake
Prevent the phone from going to sleep while a task is running.
No privacy risk; mostly an effect on the battery.
Connect to Bluetooth devices
Connect to Bluetooth devices already paired with the phone.
Reveals the list of your devices (car, watch, earbuds): a clue about your habits.
NFC
Exchange data with an NFC tag or terminal held close to the phone.
Needed for contactless payment or reading an ID document; only works at a few centimetres.
Biometric authentication
Ask you to confirm with your fingerprint or face.
Reassuring: the app never sees your fingerprint, Android only answers “yes” or “no”.
Ignore battery optimisation
Ask to escape the battery saver so it can keep running in the background.
Legitimate for a watch or messaging app; elsewhere, a sign of an app that wants to stay active permanently.
Targeting ID (Privacy Sandbox)
Read the targeting ID through Android\'s new targeting services.
Same role as the classic targeting ID: recognising you from one app to another to target you. Deleting this ID in Android\'s privacy settings cuts it off.
Campaign attribution
Measure whether content you saw or tapped elsewhere led you to install or use the app.
Links what you do in one app to what you saw in others. Android does the matching on the phone, but the companies behind it still learn the result.
Interest topics
Get the interest topics Android deduces from the apps you use (sport, travel, cooking…).
Your phone itself profiles you and hands your interests to third-party companies. You can see and switch off these topics: Settings > Privacy > Ads > Ad topics.
Custom audiences
Add you to audiences (e.g. “looked at shoes”) used to target you later in other apps.
This is retargeting: what you look at in one app follows you elsewhere. It can be switched off in the ad settings (“App-suggested ads”).
Targeting services setup
Declare which of Android\'s targeting services the app intends to use.
A sign that the app (or one of its SDKs) is ready for targeting on the phone.
Detect screenshots
Be notified when you take a screenshot of the app.
Mostly used to warn the other person in a conversation, or to protect content. The app does not see the screenshot itself.
Detect screen recording
Know when the app\'s screen is being recorded.
Protects sensitive content (bank, video); no access to the recording.
Screen recording or casting
Record or broadcast everything shown on the screen, in the background.
Messages, passwords as you type them, banking: everything on screen is captured. Android asks you each time and shows an icon while it runs; refuse if you did not ask for it.
Screen capture
Capture the content of the screen.
Reserved for the system; an ordinary app cannot obtain it.
Hide other apps\' overlays
Hide the windows other apps draw over this one.
A protection: banking apps use it to prevent a fake window from covering their screen.
Read the clipboard in the background
Read what you copied, even when you are not using the app.
You copy passwords, codes, addresses. Since Android 10 ordinary apps cannot read it in the background, and Android 12 shows a message when an app reads it.
Read screen content for the assistant
Let the assistant read what is on the screen when you call it.
Useful for “what\'s on my screen?”, but the assistant then sees your messages and pages.
Microphone in the background
Keep using the microphone after you leave the app, with a notification.
Normal for a call or a recorder. Elsewhere, an app that listens when you\'re not using it deserves your attention: a green dot shows when the mic is on.
Camera in the background
Keep using the camera after you leave the app, with a notification.
Rarely justified outside a video call or a dashcam.
Location in the background
Keep following your position after you leave the app, with a notification.
Expected for GPS navigation or recording a run. For any other app, it\'s continuous tracking.
Background sync
Keep uploading or downloading data after you leave the app.
Useful for backups and transfers; also the way data leaves the phone without you watching.
Background playback
Keep playing music or video after you leave the app.
No privacy risk: it\'s what lets your music play screen off.
Calls in the background
Keep a call going after you leave the app.
Expected for messaging and calling apps.
Connected device in the background
Stay connected to a watch, headphones or a car after you leave the app.
Expected for a companion app; elsewhere it\'s a way to keep running.
Special background use
Keep running in the background for a reason that fits no standard category.
The app must justify it to Google Play; it remains a way to escape Android\'s limits.
Exact alarms
Wake up at a precise time, even in battery-saving mode.
Normal for an alarm clock or a reminder; elsewhere a way to run regularly in the background. Revocable in Special app access.
Exact alarms (granted automatically)
Same as exact alarms, but without being able to refuse.
Google Play restricts it to alarm clocks and calendars.
Full-screen notifications
Show a notification that takes over the whole screen, even when locked.
Meant for incoming calls and alarms. Otherwise it\'s intrusive; it can be revoked in Special app access.
Long tasks you started
Finish a long task you started (download, export) in the background.
Low risk: the task must have been started by you.
Push notifications (Google)
Receive messages from the app\'s servers through Google, even when it is closed.
Essential for messaging. It also lets the app wake up remotely, and Google sees when it gets messages.
Vibrate
Make the phone vibrate.
No privacy risk.
Do Not Disturb
Read the Do Not Disturb setting and, if you allow it in Special app access, change it.
No access to your data; useful for an alarm clock or a calendar that silences the phone.
Persistent system messages
Send messages to other apps that stay available after they are sent.
An old mechanism, abandoned by Android; no privacy risk.
Live notifications
Show a notification that follows something in progress (delivery, ride, score) at the top of the screen.
No access to your data. Recent Android versions let you turn it off per app.
Download without notification
Hide the notification of a download made through Android\'s download manager.
No effect on recent Android versions, which no longer define it. It never sent your data anywhere: it only concerned files received.
Selected photos
Read only the photos and videos you pick, not the whole gallery.
The privacy-friendly way to share pictures (Android 14+): the app sees only what you select, and you can change the selection at any time.
In-app purchases
Offer purchases and subscriptions through Google Play.
No access to your bank details, which stay with Google; a sign of in-app purchases.
Fingerprint (legacy)
Ask you to confirm with your fingerprint (older version of biometric authentication).
As with biometrics, the app never sees your fingerprint.
Manage accounts
Add or remove accounts on the phone (legacy permission).
Ignored since Android 6 for other apps\' accounts; a sign of an old code base.
Control Wi-Fi
Turn Wi-Fi on or off and connect to networks.
Also allows scanning nearby networks, which can reveal your location.
Read system logs
Read the logs written by the system and other apps.
Logs can contain personal data. An ordinary app only sees its own logs unless granted from a computer.
Modify system settings
Change settings such as brightness, ringtone or screen timeout.
Not a data leak, but an app that changes your settings without asking. Revocable in Special app access.
Health Connect data
Read or write your health data in Health Connect: steps, heart rate, sleep, weight, cycle, blood glucose…
Each type of data is a separate permission that you grant in Health Connect. Some are among the most intimate (cycle, sexual activity, blood glucose): grant only what the app really needs.
Advertising

Collects your phone\'s advertising ID, your interests and how you react to ads, then auctions them to many advertisers every time an ad is shown. Your data thus travels to dozens of companies you have never heard of.
Profiling
Builds a detailed portrait of you: habits, purchases, interests, sometimes health or opinions inferred from your behaviour. These profiles are cross-referenced between apps and feed data brokers.
Location
Records your locations, often continuously, including through Bluetooth beacons in shops. They reveal home, work and sensitive places (health, worship, dating) and are almost impossible to anonymise.
Identification
Links your activity to an identity: Facebook or other account, device identifier. It becomes possible to recognise you from one app to another and tie your usage to your real name.
Analytics

Measures what you do in the app (screens viewed, taps, purchases, time spent) and sends it to a third party, often Google or Facebook, even if you have no account there. Also used to attribute your install to a marketing campaign.
Crash reporting
Sends a technical report when the app crashes: phone model, Android version, steps before the error. Useful for app quality and not very intrusive, but it still describes your device.
No known category
The Exodus database does not document what it does. To be safe, it is counted as an analytics tracker.
Uncategorised
Unknown category: no permission is presumed necessary, each one is considered unexpected.
Navigation & maps
Guidance relies on your location. Microphone (voice commands), contacts (addresses) and Bluetooth (car) are tolerated.
Transport & mobility
Timetables and routes around you. The camera (scanning a ticket) and calendar (adding a trip) are tolerated.
Connected vehicle
Locate the car and connect to it over Bluetooth. Contacts, calendar and microphone are tolerated for in-car features.
Weather
The city is enough for local weather. Precise or background location is only tolerated, for alerts.
Simple tools
A torch, calculator or compass needs nothing sensitive. The camera is tolerated for the torch, even though Android has not needed it since version 6.
Messaging & calls
Write to your contacts, send photos, videos and voice messages, make calls.
E-mail
Find recipients and attach files or photos. Calendar and microphone are tolerated.
Social networks
Post photos, videos and sounds. Finding friends and tagging a post\'s location are only tolerated.
Audio, video & streaming
Play your music and videos. Bluetooth (speakers) and microphone (music recognition) are tolerated.
News & reading
Reading articles requires no sensitive permission. The city is tolerated for local news.
Shopping & e-commerce
Scan a product and photograph a listing. Location, to find a nearby shop or listing, is tolerated.
Banking, payment & customer accounts
Scan a cheque or an ID document. Reading your SMS is unnecessary: Android passes on verification codes without giving access to them.
Health (admin, appointments, insurance)
Send a prescription or a receipt as a photo. Calendar and location are tolerated for appointments.
Watch / wearable companion
Pair and sync the watch: Bluetooth, sensors, activity, location. SMS and calls are tolerated to show them on your wrist.
Sport & fitness
Track your routes and efforts: location, activity, sensors, Bluetooth for a heart-rate strap.
Security, authentication & identity
Scan a QR code to add an account. Accessibility is tolerated for password autofill.
Web browser
A browser asks nothing for itself: it relays requests from websites (camera, microphone, location), hence a simple tolerance.
AI assistants
Talk to the assistant and show it pictures. Calendar, contacts and location are only tolerated.
Office, cloud & dev
Open, scan and sync your files and photos.
Photo, video & galleries
Take and manage your photos and videos, connect to a camera over Bluetooth or Wi-Fi.
Travel, outings & events
Find places and events around you. Calendar and photos are tolerated for bookings.
Games
A game needs no sensitive permission. Microphone and Bluetooth are tolerated for voice chat and controllers.
Accessibility
Reading the screen and acting for you is precisely their job: accessibility and microphone are justified.
Health tracking (cycle, glucose, blood pressure)
Personal medical tracking: it needs intimate health data, and nothing else.
Dating
Profiles, photos and proximity: the city is enough, and your address book has no business here.
Keyboards
A keyboard sees everything you type: it should ask for nothing more than the microphone, for dictation.
School, family & discovery
Send homework or documents as photos. The calendar is tolerated for the timetable.
